newsitem.title: USA: AOL hit with suit charging insider trading.
newsitem.headline: AOL hit with suit charging insider trading.

text.p: Two law firms sued America Online Inc. on behalf of shareholders Monday, accusing executives of the world's No. 1 online service, including Chairman Steve Case, of insider trading.

The lawsuit alleges that America Online officers, directors and outside accountants violated federal securities laws. They said the 18 defendants sold shares in the company at a profit before October, when the company announced losses and a big charge for changes in its accounting practices.

The lawsuit was filed in U.S. District Court in Alexandria, Va., by New York-based law firm Milberg Weiss and a Wilmington, Del.-based firm, Morris and Morris on behalf of purchasers of America Online stock from Aug. 10, 1995, to Oct. 29, 1996.
The lawsuit alleges the 18 insiders "took advantage of the artificial inflation in America Online's stock," which peaked at $71 a share in May 1996.

America Online had been deferring hundreds of millions of dollars in costs of getting new subscribers, which the lawsuit says was represented by America Online as certified by accountants Ernst & Young as conforming with generally accepted accounting principles.
An AOL spokeswoman said, "We are confident that we acted in full compliance with all applicable securities laws."
She pointed out that the percentages of actual stock sold quoted in the lawsuit did not take into consideration the total number of shares available to executives in stock option plans.

The lawsuit said America Online co-founder and Chairman Emeritus James Kimsey sold 82 percent of his America Online stock, or 651,000 shares, at prices as high as $55.375 a share, for $24.5 million. America Online co-founder and Chairman Case sold 76 percent of his AOL stock, or 575,000 shares, at prices as high as $55 a share, for a total of $29.1 million, the lawsuit said.
Chief Financial Officer Lennert Leader sold 66 percent of his America Online stock, or 210,800 shares, at prices as high as $54 a share, for a total of $10 million, the lawsuit said.
The lawsuit said America Online's ensuing accounting changes, its losses and its financial charges helped fuel a drop in its stock price from June to October 1996.
America Online stock rose 62.5 cents to $35.50 in consolidated trading Monday on the New York Stock Exchange.
